name: Contrast theory

lead: Contrast theory says that faces with strong tonal difference between the skin and the eyes, lips and brows tend to read as healthier, younger and more attractive. Looksmaxxers use it to explain why some hair, skin and eye colour combinations stand out, and to guide choices such as hair dye, brow darkness or makeup.

A published line of research by psychologist Richard Russell and colleagues supports the starting point: facial contrast differs between sexes and has been linked to perceived health. Forum versions go further and apply the idea to hair-versus-eye contrast and complexion rules that have not been tested as stated.

paras: In practice people compare their own skin, hair, brow and eye tones, look at photos for how defined the eyes, brows and lips appear, and adjust things such as hair colour, brow shade, tan, or makeup. Discussions on looksmax.org use before-and-after photos and example faces.

The theory is a perceptual idea, not a procedure, so direct harms are limited to those of whatever is used to alter contrast, such as hair dye, tanning or cosmetics. Community rules of thumb are anecdotal and individual preferences vary.

angle.text: People adjust brow, hair, makeup or tan so the eyes and lips stand out against the skin. Research links higher facial contrast with perceived health and with a feminine appearance, so approaches differ between sexes.

lead: Contrast theory, in looksmaxxing usage, holds that the tonal contrast between the skin and the facial features such as eyes, brows and lips contributes to how attractive and healthy a face appears. It is part of the broader discussion of colouring and complexion (coloringmaxxing) on forums such as looksmax.org [1][2].

Academic work gives the idea an empirical basis. Richard Russell reported in 2009 that female faces have more contrast between the eyes, lips and surrounding skin than male faces, mostly because female skin is lighter, and that altering contrast alone could shift an androgynous face towards looking male or female [3]. He suggested that makeup, which tends to raise contrast, may work partly by exaggerating this sex-linked cue [3]. A 2016 paper by Russell and colleagues found that facial contrast predicts perceived health and that increasing contrast made faces look healthier [4].

Community versions are broader. A looksmax.org thread asks whether hair darker than the eyes is a good rule of thumb for contrast, and a multi-part coloring guide also discusses research on red and attractiveness [1][2].

paras: Russell, a psychology professor at Gettysburg College, published a study in Perception in 2009 showing that facial contrast carries information about sex: women's faces have greater luminance contrast among the eyes, lips and surrounding skin, and people unconsciously use this when judging sex [3]. He noted that cosmetics generally increase this contrast and proposed that they may work partly by making a face appear more feminine, which correlates with attractiveness [3].

Russell, Porcheron, Sweda, Jones, Mauger and Morizot reported in 2016 that facial contrast predicted perceived health from the face, and in two further experiments that participants perceived faces with increased contrast as healthier [4]. Earlier work on contrast around the lips and health, by Stephen and colleagues, found only one of three contrast aspects related to perceived health, as noted by Russell's team [4].

On looksmax.org, contrast is discussed alongside colouring: threads propose hair darker than eyes as a rule, and post example photos to illustrate high and low contrast [1]. A long guide splits the topic into parts and cites popular articles on red and attractiveness, including claims that red enhances ratings of men by women, and links skin redness to blood flow as a possible signal [2]. Some replies in these threads argue about other traits, such as preferences for blond hair, which shows the idea is applied loosely [1].

No studies found testing the community form of contrast theory (hair-eye contrast rules). Laboratory perception studies of facial contrast exist: the 2009 study on sex perception [3] and the 2016 studies on perceived health [4].

lore.intro: Forum users apply contrast to hair, eye and skin combinations, often with side-by-side photos [1][2].
